name: Ondategiko Haritza (the Roble de Ondategi / Roble de Sarragoa)
age_estimate: documented only as "centenario" (very old); no numeric age given by any source

location.address: On the campa (communal meadow) of Sarragoa, at the southwest edge of Ondategi, at the end of the street to the left of the church, Zigoitia, Alava/Araba
location.neighbourhood: Ondategi, a small village of Zigoitia municipality, Alava/Araba

access: Free. Stands on an open communal meadow (campa) at the village edge, reached by the street that runs left of the church; no gate, ticket or private-land caveat found in any source. Also known locally as the Roble de Sarragoa / Sarragoako haritza / Arbol gordo de Zanagua.
transport: Rural Zigoitia, Alava; no realistic public transport. About 13km from Vitoria-Gasteiz (unpublished) and 38km from Bilbao (published); a car is the realistic way to reach it.
story:
Until the Spanish Civil War, the village of Ondategi held its summer festival under this oak, and the music was one accordion. The San Lorenzo romería fell on 10 August, and the village could afford paid musicians for only one feast a year, Santa Lucía on 13 December. So in August a single accordionist played in the shade of the Sarragoa oak, and that was the party.

The tree has the room for it. It is a pedunculate oak 20 metres tall with a crown about 30 metres across, standing on the campa of Sarragoa, the communal meadow at the southwest edge of the village, at the end of the street that runs to the left of the church. For generations it gave shade and shelter to livestock and people alike. The Basque Government declared it a Singular Tree in 1997, one of ten in Álava, and the published measurement puts the trunk at 4.9 metres round at chest height.

Locally it goes by several names: Ondategiko Haritza, Sarragoako haritza, the Roble de Sarragoa, and the plainer Árbol gordo de Zanagua, the fat tree. Every source calls it centenario, which means old and nothing more precise. Nobody has published an age, and a trunk of that size does not settle it on its own. If you know when the romería under it began, that would be a start.

The romería under its crown did not survive the war. The oak did.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its spread: an oak with a crown about 30 metres wide and a trunk 4.9 metres round, on the open meadow at the end of the street left of Ondategi's church.

name: Olmo centenario de Millena (Om centenari de Millena)

location.address: Plaza de la Iglesia de Sant Josep, Millena, El Comtat, Alicante province, Comunitat Valenciana
location.neighbourhood: Church square (Plaza de la Iglesia), village centre of Millena

access: Free. Stands in the open church square (Plaza de la Iglesia de Sant Josep) in the centre of the small village of Millena (population around 200); lacantimploraverde.es describes it as easy to find, with the village itself putting up signage pointing visitors to it at the entrance to town.
transport: Rural inland Alicante province (El Comtat comarca), between Gorga and Cocentaina; no public transport reaches the village. Roughly 65km from Alicante city (published) and well outside any day-trip boundary from it; realistically reached by car, e.g. from Cocentaina or Alcoi (neither currently published).
story:
Dutch elm disease killed the village elms of Alicante province one square at a time, and by two independent accounts this is the last healthy one still standing in a plaza. It grows in front of the Church of Sant Josep in Millena, a village of around two hundred people in El Comtat, and the village signposts it at the entrance to town.

Locally it is the Om mil·lenari, the thousand-year elm. It is not that old. The published estimates say about three hundred years, and one travel writer who visited suggests it may be younger still: elms were planted in Spanish town squares to mark the Cádiz Constitution of 1812, and he wonders whether this is one of them. That is his theory rather than a record, so hold both ideas loosely, somewhere between two and three centuries.

The measurements are firmer. The trunk is 5.30 metres round, the tree about ten metres tall with a crown up to eleven metres across, which is a great deal of wood for a field elm. Some of it has proved too heavy. A limb broke under snow, pillars were added to hold up the rest, and a later snowfall damaged one of the pillars.

It is not on the Valencian catalogue of monumental trees, but it is protected under the region's 2006 law on monumental trees. The most recent account we found is from 2016. If you have been since, tell us how it looks.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the support pillars propping up its heavy limbs and a trunk 5.30 metres round. It stands in the church square in front of the Church of Sant Josep, in the centre of Millena.
